notes.meaning: Moses now turns from general teaching to specific rules. He begins with rules about how to worship God. They were to keep these all their lives, not just in hard times but also when they were settled and doing well in the land.

The people of Canaan worshiped their gods on mountains, on hills and under shady trees. They thought being up high or in a quiet grove brought them closer to their gods. Israel was to destroy every such place. That way nothing would be left to tempt them later.

Every altar, stone pillar, wooden pole and idol had to go. Even the names had to be wiped out, because hills and valleys were often named after the gods worshiped there. Naming a place after a god was a way of claiming it. Erasing the name cancelled that claim.

Israel must not worship the true God the way the nations worshiped their idols. That meant no altars on any hill or under any tree they liked. They also must not borrow pagan customs, even to try to make worship better. God is above all gods and will not be worshiped like them.

God himself, not the people, would choose one place to "put his Name." That meant the place where he would show his presence and be worshiped. This was where the ark rested: first Shiloh, and later Jerusalem. Having one place kept the tribes united. It also pointed to one God and one way to come to him, which Christians see fulfilled in Christ. The place was not named yet, perhaps so the tribes would not quarrel over it.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think the rule of one place of sacrifice came later than Moses. They suggest it may have grown out of Jerusalem priests' demands after the Temple was built, partly to shut down corrupt local shrines.

notes.meaning: All kinds of gifts were to come to that one place. These included burnt offerings, other sacrifices, tithes (a tenth of their produce), firstfruits, vows, freewill gifts and firstborn animals. The people could choose what to give freely, but not where to give it. These offerings had no worth in themselves. Their value came from God's altar, which pointed ahead to Christ.

At God's place, families would eat part of their offerings as a holy meal "before the LORD." This was a feast with God, not just an ordinary dinner. They were to rejoice because God had blessed their work. Serving God was meant to be a joy, not a chore.

In the wilderness, life was unsettled and always on the move. Many things could not be done in the proper order, and God allowed some freedom then. This is not mainly about open idol worship. It means things were looser than they should be. Once they were settled, that would no longer be allowed.
The reason for the looser ways was simple. Israel had not yet reached its "rest," the promised land. Some see Canaan as a picture of the heavenly rest still waiting for believers.

Once they crossed the Jordan and God gave them peace from their enemies, he would choose his place. Then all their offerings must go there. Winning battles was not enough; they needed God to keep them safe. That full rest did not really come until King David's time. The "choice" vows means their best gifts.

The whole household was to share the joy: sons, daughters and servants. Women were welcome too, even though only men were required to come to the feasts. The Levites were the tribe set apart to serve in worship. They owned no land, so they were to be invited to share the feast.

They must not offer sacrifices just anywhere a place looked pretty or holy to them. Burnt offerings stand here for all the offerings. Keeping to one place stopped each person from making up their own worship. It also protected the meaning of the rituals, which pointed to the coming Messiah.

In the wilderness, animals for food had to be killed at the tabernacle. In the land, people could slaughter and eat meat at home. This kind of meat was treated like gazelle or deer, which were never offered as sacrifices. So even someone who was "ceremonially unclean" (not fit for holy meals for a time) could eat it. They were to eat "according to the blessing," living within their means.
The one firm rule was this: do not eat the blood. It was to be poured on the ground. This rule goes back to God's word to Noah after the flood. It also taught respect for life.

Anything set apart for God could not be eaten at home. This included tithes of grain, wine and oil, firstborn animals, vows and gifts. These were eaten only at God's chosen place. The tithe here is often understood as a "second tithe" used for these holy feasts. The whole household, including servants and the local Levite, would rejoice together there.

Israel must never neglect the Levites, who had no land of their own. Today this reminds believers to care for the ministers who teach them well. People who serve God's people should have what they need to live.

As God widened their land, many would live far from his place. They could not bring every animal there. So God freely allowed them to eat meat whenever they wished. He did not grudge them good food, though they should enjoy it with self-control.

Distance from God's place is the reason for this new freedom. It replaced the wilderness rule that all animals be killed at the tabernacle. "As I have commanded" means killing the animal so the blood is drained out.
Meat killed at home was ordinary food, like deer, not a sacrifice. Because it was not holy food, both clean and unclean people could eat it. This does not mean they had to eat at the same table.

"Be sure" can mean "be strong." Hold firm against the temptation to eat blood, which the other nations ate freely. Blood stands for the life of the animal. That life was given on the altar for atonement, meaning the covering of sin so people could be at peace with God.
The blood was poured on the ground as something that did not belong to them. Life belongs to God, the one who gives it. The earth soaked it up.
The command is repeated again to show how much it mattered. Obeying it was doing right in God's eyes. God promised it would go well with them and their children.
Ordinary meat could be eaten at home. But holy gifts and vow offerings still had to be taken to God's chosen place. One altar kept worship pure. Many altars would soon lead to many gods.

A burnt offering went wholly on the altar, meat and blood. With other sacrifices, such as fellowship offerings, the blood went to the altar. After God's portion and the priest's share, the worshiper could eat the meat.

Moses urges them to obey all these things, so it would go well with them and their children. God binds himself by promise to do good to those who obey. He owes us nothing, yet he faithfully rewards obedience.

After God drove out the nations, Israel must not be trapped by their ways. They should not even ask how those nations worshiped. People then believed that ignoring a land's local gods brought bad luck, so the pull was strong. Curiosity about false worship is often where idolatry begins. And it makes no sense to copy people whose gods could not save them.
Their worship was full of things God hates. They even burned their own children to gods like Molech. Bringing such customs into God's worship would turn the worship itself into something God hates.

Moses closes by saying: do what God commands, adding nothing and taking nothing away. Worship is to follow God's word, not our own ideas. This verse also leads into chapter 13's warnings about people who tempt others to idolatry.

differ.view: This verse supports the belief that God may be worshiped only in ways Scripture commands. Anything not commanded should be left out.
Obedience matters greatly. But Deuteronomy itself adapts earlier laws, so the Bible's truths must be applied afresh in each age.
